stories.title: Generations at the forge
stories.summary: The Harrisons’ forge on Church Street made and mended almost everything the village needed.
stories.body:
For generations the village forge was where things got made and mended. Its blacksmiths shod horses, but they also made cart wheels, gates and ironmongery for farms and households all over the parish.

The forge was on Church Street and was run by the Harrison family. A photograph from 1926 shows the blacksmith at work at Harrison’s Forge, and decades later, when the village’s old fire pump was restored, one of its wooden wheels was repaired at “Harrison’s Church Street Blacksmiths”.

The forge also shows how village trades changed with the times. A Bulletin exhibition notice describes a shop where you could have your horse shod, your wireless accumulator charged or your bike brakes fixed, all in one place.
stories.source: East Hendred Bulletin, Spring 2016 (no. 144) and Winter 2015 (no. 143), East Hendred Parish Council; Hendred Museum, ‘The Fire Pump’, https://www.hendredmuseum.org.uk/fire-pump

stories.title: The day the evacuees came
stories.summary: On 1 September 1939 London schoolboys from West Ham arrived to sit out the war in the village.
stories.body:
On 1 September 1939, two days before Britain declared war on Germany, a party of evacuee children from London arrived in East Hendred. Among them were boys from Cave Road School in West Ham, in the East End.

Their arrival changed village life overnight. The village school suddenly had to make room for them, and accounts suggest local children and evacuees took turns, with the village children in school in the mornings.

Some stayed on. A 2006 Bulletin mentions a village family who first came to Hendred as evacuees, and decades after the war the Bulletin was still appealing for former evacuees to get in touch for a reunion.
stories.people: Boys of Cave Road School, West Ham
stories.source: East Hendred Bulletin, Summer 2004 (no. 102); Winter 2015 (no. 143); Autumn 2006 (no. 107); Hendred Museum WW2 exhibition (2025–26)

stories.title: Lessons at Snells Hall
stories.summary: The village hall was the village school for over a century, with a famously strict headmaster.
stories.body:
Snells Hall, today the village hall, began life as the Church of England school, built and opened in 1860. It taught village children for over a century, until 1967, when the school moved to new premises shared with West Hendred.

Stan Francis, born in 1928, started there in 1933. He remembered the headmaster, Bertram Everest Newman, who ran the school from 1900 to 1936 and again from 1939 to 1945, as a strict disciplinarian, in an age when the cane was normal.

The war turned school life upside down. Robin Hine has described how lessons changed when evacuees from East London arrived in 1939 and the school had to make room for them.
stories.people: Stan Francis; Robin Hine; Bertram Everest Newman (headmaster)
stories.source: East Hendred Bulletin, Winter 2015 (no. 143), school history by Tessa Case; East Hendred Bulletin, Autumn 2025; ‘West Hendred’, Wikipedia (1967 school merger)

stories.title: Halfpennies at Wilkins
stories.summary: Older villagers remember spending their halfpennies at Wilkins Shop.
stories.body:
Ask older villagers about childhood treats and you may hear about Wilkins Shop, where children spent their halfpennies.

In a village with no through road, the shop was one of the places where everyone’s day crossed. Memories like this were gathered for the Bulletin’s local history exhibitions, and the Hendred Museum would like to hear from anyone who remembers what Wilkins sold, or who ran it.

stories.title: A family of carpenters
stories.summary: Joseph Hunt, born 1771, began several generations of Hunt carpenters in the village.
stories.body:
Joseph Hunt was born in East Hendred in 1771. He is the first of his family to be recorded in the village as a carpenter, and several generations of Hunts followed him into the trade.

In a village of timber-framed cottages, barns and farm carts, a carpenter’s work never ran out.
stories.source: ‘The Hunts of East Hendred’, family history website, https://freepages.rootsweb.com/~hendred/genealogy/Hunts.htm

stories.title: The parson who wrote home
stories.summary: Rector George Woodward’s letters to his uncle give a rare look inside a Georgian parsonage.
stories.body:
George Woodward was rector of East Hendred from the 1750s until he died on 5 May 1790. He lived at the rectory opposite the church: a timber-framed house later enlarged in red brick, with remarkable yew hedges in its garden.

Between 1753 and 1761 he wrote a long run of letters to his uncle. They are mostly about himself and his family rather than the village, but they give a rare, informal picture of a Georgian country parson’s household. He wrote without paragraphs, in one long flow.

He left a mark in the church too. Among the church plate, a flagon and alms dish are inscribed ‘Ex dono Geo. Woodward Rector 1783’: a gift from the rector in 1783.

The letters were edited by Donald Gibson and published in 1982 as A Parson in the Vale of White Horse.
stories.place: The rectory, opposite St Augustine’s Church
stories.source: D. Gibson (ed.), A Parson in the Vale of White Horse: George Woodward’s Letters from East Hendred 1753–1761 (Alan Sutton, 1982); ‘Parishes: East Hendred’, in A History of the County of Berkshire, vol. 4, ed. W. Page and P.H. Ditchfield (Victoria County History, 1924), pp. 294–302, https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/berks/vol4/pp294-302; J. Foster, Alumni Oxonienses 1715–1886, vol. 4, p. 414

stories.title: Keeping the faceless clock
stories.summary: Made in 1525, wound by hand for centuries, overhauled in 1961 and restored again for its 500th birthday.
stories.body:
St Augustine’s clock was made in 1525 by John Seymour of Wantage, whose name and the date are still inscribed on part of the works. It has no dial and no hands. It tells the time by striking, and every three hours from nine in the morning it plays a hymn tune, the Angels’ Song, usually credited to Orlando Gibbons.

For centuries someone climbed the tower to wind it by hand every day. In 1961 Arthur Harrison overhauled it, and the Hendred Museum says it has kept very good time since.

In 2024, ahead of its 500th birthday, the clock was restored again and given automatic winding. The village celebrated Clock500 in 2025 with tower tours, and the BBC reported on the clock still keeping the village on time after five centuries.
stories.people: John Seymour of Wantage; Arthur Harrison; Simon Gilchrist (horologist)
stories.source: ‘Parishes: East Hendred’, in A History of the County of Berkshire, vol. 4, ed. W. Page and P.H. Ditchfield (Victoria County History, 1924), pp. 294–302, https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/berks/vol4/pp294-302; Hendred Museum, ‘Points of interest’, https://www.hendredmuseum.org.uk/points-of-interest; ‘East Hendred’, Wikipedia (citing BBC News, ‘Oxfordshire clock still keeping village on time after 500 years’, 28 May 2025); C.F.C. Beeson, Clockmaking in Oxfordshire 1400–1850 (3rd edn, 1989), p. 20

stories.title: The physicist on Cat Street
stories.summary: William Penney, leader of Britain’s atomic programme, lived at Orchard House and took the village’s name.
stories.body:
William Penney (1909–1991) was the mathematician and physicist who led Britain’s atomic weapons programme. He worked at Los Alamos during the Second World War, and later headed the Atomic Weapons Research Establishment and the UK Atomic Energy Authority, whose Harwell site sits on the edge of the parish.

He made his home at Orchard House on Cat Street. When he was made a life peer in 1967 he took the title Baron Penney, of East Hendred, and he died in the village on 3 March 1991.

In later life he admitted to qualms about his work, though he maintained it had been necessary. A blue plaque was unveiled at Orchard House on 8 August 2014.
stories.source: ‘William Penney, Baron Penney’, Wikipedia; Oxfordshire Blue Plaques Board, ‘William Penney’, http://oxonblueplaques.org.uk/plaques/penney.html

stories.title: Ghosts without feet
stories.summary: Civil War soldiers seen in a village cottage, but only from the ankles up.
stories.body:
After one of the Civil War battles at Newbury in the 1640s, Parliamentarian soldiers are said to have been billeted in East Hendred.

Three centuries later, in the 1940s, people in one village cottage reported ghostly Roundhead soldiers, visible only from the ankles up. The explanation offered was simple: the floor had been raised since the 1600s, so the soldiers walked on the old floor level, their feet hidden beneath the new one.

The story doesn’t record which cottage it was.
stories.source: Royal Berkshire History, ‘East Hendred’ (Nash Ford Publishing, 2001), https://www.berkshirehistory.com/villages/easthendred.html

stories.title: The cloth fairs of the Golden Mile
stories.summary: Tradition says Hendred’s medieval cloth fairs were held on a green lane called the Golden Mile.
stories.body:
In the 15th century East Hendred grew rich on cloth, rich enough to be called a town. Brasses in the church remember its wool merchants: the brothers Henry and Roger Eldysley (Roger died in 1439), shown with their merchants’ marks, and William Whitwey (1479), described in Latin as a draper and woolman.

Village tradition says the cloth fairs were held on a green lane known as the Golden Mile, and links certain grass terraces in the centre of the village with the trade. Nobody has proved it, but the name has stuck.

There were real fairs too. In 1415 Henry V granted the Prior of Sheen a Tuesday market and two fairs here, around St Augustine’s day (26 May) and St Katherine’s (25 November). They never really flourished.
stories.people: Henry and Roger Eldysley; William Whitwey
stories.source: ‘Parishes: East Hendred’, in A History of the County of Berkshire, vol. 4, ed. W. Page and P.H. Ditchfield (Victoria County History, 1924), pp. 294–302, https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/berks/vol4/pp294-302

stories.title: A king’s revenge at Cwichelm’s mound
stories.summary: A botched assassination, a royal revenge, and a king who may or may not lie under Scutchamer Knob.
stories.body:
Cwichelm was a 7th-century king of the Gewisse, the people who became the West Saxons. The historian Bede says that around 626 Cwichelm sent an assassin to kill King Edwin of Northumbria. The attempt failed.

A much later chronicle, written at St Albans in the 13th century, claims Edwin took his revenge by killing Cwichelm at the mound on the downs that bears his name: Cwichelm’s barrow, now Scutchamer Knob. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle tells a different story, in which Cwichelm was baptised at Dorchester in 636 and died the same year.

The mound is older than either king. It is an early Iron Age barrow, and digs have found no burial. The legend of a king beneath it has lasted anyway.
stories.people: King Cwichelm of the Gewisse; King Edwin of Northumbria
stories.source: ‘Cwichelm of Wessex’, Wikipedia (citing Bede and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle); Royal Berkshire History, ‘East Hendred’; ‘Scutchamer Knob’, Wikipedia; Historic England list entry 1006312

stories.title: The Danes take a dare
stories.summary: In 1006 a Viking army marched to Cwichelm’s barrow to defy a prophecy, then went home anyway.
stories.body:
In the winter of 1006 a Danish army raiding Wessex marched up to Cwichelm’s barrow on the Berkshire Downs. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle explains why: it had long been said that if they ever reached the mound, they would never get back to the sea.

They reached it, waited there as if daring the prophecy to come true, and then went back to the sea by another way. The Chronicle’s account of that year records the barrow by its old name, Cwichelmeshlæw.
stories.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, annal for 1006 (as summarised in ‘Scutchamer Knob’, Wikipedia, and the Victoria County History, Berkshire vol. 4, p. 294)
